The lighthouse keeper lived on the island for forty years, long after the light no longer needed keeping. Automation arrived one spring, replacing brass gears and oil lamps with circuits that never slept. They left him a cottage, a pension, and a promise nobody quite remembered making. He stayed anyway.

Each evening he climbed the iron stairs, not because the lamp required him, but because climbing had become the shape of his days. One hundred and twelve steps. He knew each by sound, by cold iron singing under his boots, by the curve of the banister, worn smooth by hands.

At the top he opened the service door, listened to the hum of the lens turning, and watched the beam sweep the dark sea. Ships passed now. Shipping lanes had moved east toward deeper water. Sometimes a fishing boat blinked away, but the dark belonged to seals, gulls, and storms.

He kept a logbook. Weather. Wind. What he ate. Whether the radio worked. The entries grew shorter over years, until some days held three words: Clear. Cold. Alone. He liked the honesty of that. The sea did not bargain, and neither, he decided, should he. Truth was simpler than tales.

In October a girl arrived on the supply boat, curious about the old man who still climbed the tower. She found him polishing a lens that no longer shone. He showed her how to read the beam's rhythm, how to tell time by its return. She asked why he stayed.
